Meaning was defined by Aristotle [[46]] as "Telos" [[5]] or a "Final end or Purpose" of Function [[40]]. In the Context of "Lzahlia's Philosophy of Systems" [[27]] Meaning plays the Central role of sufficing Reason [[]], while Function...

The following study attempts to unravel the interconnected weavings between Function [[40]] and Meaning [[41]] in General-Systems [[38]] and in Human [[63]] life.

Meaning is immaterial [[25]] and Subjective [[59]]; It essentially cannot be measured or proven by Empirical [[61]] means. While Meaning cannot be measured statistically; it has been argued by Philosophers [[47]] for Centuries; that Meaning is necessary for the Human Being [[63]] 

Psychologically [[86]] Meaning [[41]] is also fundamental to Human [[63]] Well-being.

Meaning is also proposed as the bridge between living systems and the mechanical.

For the living being, meaning provides "Reason" [[10]] to Function [[40]]

The central case for "Meaning and Function" are described by a Paradox [[84]]; Meaning is incomplete without use. While function is incomplete without meaning. Figuratively speaking, in the case of 1000s of memories, as meaningful they may be; even in the Human-Neuron-Biota [[16]] does not process all as equals; certain memories are prioritized over others by complex Neurological Processess [[74]]. These complex means are generalizable as a System of Values [[3]]

A machine [[72]] does not require meaning. The machine's primary function is not a purpose but a function itself; to execute instructions (at the mechanical level, Information may be Decoupled from meaning [[14]].) Yet, in order for Information, Power and Eventual Practicality to be measurable by the Human; Power and Practicality must be weighted against a system of values [[3]] In other words; raw information is as radioactive power; fundamental power awaiting proper use as a contiuation of it's lifecycle [[15]].
